title: Primitive line in a nonzero induced module of a Borel character
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and $S$ a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], with semisimple and simply connected as defined in [lem-sfb-rho-section-modules]. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq S$, a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$, and its unipotent radical $U$, with these notions as in [lem-sfb-rho-section-modules]. Multiplication $T\times_F U\to B$ is an isomorphism of $F$-schemes (so each $b\in B(A)$ is uniquely $tu$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$). Write $\Phi^+$ for the positive roots specified there. There is a Weyl group element $w_0$ carrying $\Phi^+$ onto $-\Phi^+$; the Weyl group is $N_S(T)(F)/T(F)$, where $N_S(T)$ is the subgroup scheme normalizing $T$. Its action on characters is $(w\lambda)(t)=\lambda(n^{-1}tn)$ for a representative $n$ of $w$. Let $\lambda:B\to\mathbf G_m$ be a character trivial on $U$, and use the same notation for its restriction to $T$. Define
$$E_B(\lambda)=\{f\in F[S]:f(gb)=\lambda(b)^{-1}f(g)\text{ after every commutative }F\text{-algebra extension}\}$$
with rational left-translation action $(s f)(g)=f(s^{-1}g)$. If $E_B(\lambda)\ne0$, its subspace fixed by $U$ is one-dimensional, and $T$ acts on this line by the character $w_0\lambda$. Here fixed means the coaction identity $f\mapsto f\otimes1$, and a $T$-weight $\mu$ means $t f=\mu(t)f$ after every commutative $F$-algebra extension; thus the assertion is about group schemes, not just their Lie algebras.

source.place: Definition 22.21 and Proposition 22.22 with its proof, printed pp.468--469; w_0 in Definition 21.72 and Theorem 21.73(b), printed p.448. The proposition works over any characteristic; E(lambda) need not be simple. The Borel decomposition is Remark 21.74, printed p.448, and the split solvable-group decomposition used there. See also Proposition 21.29 and its proof, printed pp.433--434 (P(lambda)=U(lambda) semidirect T).

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], $S$ is reductive and $B=U\rtimes T$. The stated $T\times U$ decomposition follows by rewriting $ut=t(t^{-1}ut)$, with inverse obtained from the projection $B\to T$. Apply [lem-sfb-longest-weyl-open-cell] to obtain $w_0$, a representative $n_0$, and the dense open immersion $j(u,b)=un_0b$. Put $E=E_B(\lambda)$. Its defining right-equivariance identity is preserved by left translation, since $(sf)(gb)=f(s^{-1}gb)=\lambda(b)^{-1}f(s^{-1}g)$ after every scalar extension. Hence the left regular coaction restricts to $E$: equivalently, $E$ is the kernel of the difference between the right-translation coaction and $f\mapsto f\otimes\lambda^{-1}$, and left and right translations commute. Tensoring kernels with vector spaces over $F$ preserves kernels, as follows by choosing bases and taking direct sums of the same kernel. Thus $E$ is a rational $U$-module without any finite-dimensionality assumption.

source.place: Proposition 22.22, first sentence of proof; 21.73(b), 21.74 and 21.84; Definition 22.21 for the regular subrepresentation.

proof.text: Both $S$ and $U$ are smooth over $F$, so [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] makes them reduced (apply the geometric-fibre assertion to their structure maps to $\operatorname{Spec}F$). The source of $j$ and its target are affine; $j$ is therefore quasi-compact and quasi-separated, as affine-locally it is a map between spectra. By [lemma-nagata-reduced-dense-image-schematic], its scheme-theoretic image is $S$. In [def-nagata-scheme-theoretic-image] the kernel ideal for a quasi-compact morphism is the actual kernel of the structure-sheaf map. It follows that $j^*:F[S]\to F[U\times B]$ is injective. Define $r:E\to F[U]$ by $r(f)(x)=f(xn_0)$. Right equivariance gives $j^*f(x,b)=\lambda(b)^{-1}r(f)(x)$ as a regular-function identity. If $r(f)=0$, this identity gives $j^*f=0$, hence $f=0$. Thus $r$ is injective. Direct substitution also gives $r(uf)(x)=r(f)(u^{-1}x)$ after every scalar extension.

source.place: Proposition 22.22, restriction to the open cell and left-translation identity; the schematic-density justification is explicit. Milne Proposition 1.10 supplies the reduced-density principle.

proof.text:
Choose $0
e h\in E$. By [lem-sfb-comodule-finite-subrepresentation] for the rational $U$-module $E$, there is a nonzero finite-dimensional rational $U$-submodule $M$ containing $h$. Choose a basis, identifying $M$ with $F^d$ for $d\ge1$. The radical $U$ is smooth affine of finite type and has a faithful representation with unipotent geometric points, by the meaning of unipotent in the hypotheses. Thus [lem-sfb-unipotent-rational-representation-fixed-vector] gives $0
e v\in M$ fixed by every $u\in U(F)$. This cited result asserts pointwise fixedness only. To obtain the coaction identity, write $ho_M(v)-v\otimes1=\sum_{i=1}^d e_i\otimes a_i$ with $a_i\in F[U]$. Every $a_i$ vanishes on all $U(F)$. Since $F[U]$ is reduced and finitely generated, clause 2 of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] gives $a_i=0$ for every $i$. Hence $ho_M(v)=v\otimes1$, and the inclusion of the subcomodule gives $0
e v\in E^U$. This step uses no characteristic-zero hypothesis.

source.place: Proposition 22.22, assertion E(lambda)^U is nonzero; Proposition 4.7/Corollary 4.8, section 14.b and Proposition 14.3. Milne Proposition 1.10 justifies upgrading fixed F-points to the coaction identity.

proof.text: For $f\in E^U$, the translation identity gives $r(f)(u^{-1}x)=r(f)(x)$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $u,x\in U(A)$. Substituting $u=x$ gives $r(f)(x)=r(f)(1)$. In particular take $A=F[U]$ and the universal point $x$; this proves $r(f)=r(f)(1)\,1$ in the coordinate algebra, rather than merely on $F$-points. The injectivity of $r$ now makes $f\mapsto r(f)(1)=f(n_0)$ an injective linear map $E^U\to F$. Together with the nonzero vector of step 3, this makes $E^U$ one-dimensional: the image of that vector is a nonzero scalar, so it spans the one-dimensional target and the inverse image of that span is all of $E^U$.

source.place: Proposition 22.22, constancy of f_U and the one-dimensionality conclusion.

proof.text:
Let $f\in E^U$, $A$ any commutative $F$-algebra, $t\in T(A)$ and $x\in U(A)$. Normality of $U$ in $B$ gives $t^{-1}xt\in U(A)$. Directly,
$$r(tf)(x)=f(t^{-1}xn_0)=f((t^{-1}xt)n_0(n_0^{-1}t^{-1}n_0))=(w_0\lambda)(t)\,r(f)(t^{-1}xt).$$
Here $n_0^{-1}t^{-1}n_0\in T(A)$, and right equivariance contributes $\lambda(n_0^{-1}t^{-1}n_0)^{-1}=\lambda(n_0^{-1}tn_0)=(w_0\lambda)(t)$, so the inverse in the definition has been accounted for. Since $r(f)$ is constant, this equals $(w_0\lambda)(t)r(f)(x)$. The map $A\otimes_F E\to A\otimes_F F[U]$ induced by $r$ is injective: extend an $F$-basis of its image to a basis of $F[U]$ to construct a linear left inverse of $r$, then tensor that inverse with $A$. The displayed equality therefore implies $tf=(w_0\lambda)(t)f$ in $A\otimes_F E$. As it holds for every $A$ and $t$, it is exactly the claimed group-scheme weight identity on the line.
